These exercises also help assess the readiness of personnel and systems, ensuring that the military can maintain operations in diverse, high-pressure scenarios. Congressionally mandated energy resilience readiness exercises (e.g., black-start exercises) could be expanded in duration (currently limited to 8 hours or less, which does not account for factors such as shift changes, changing mission-essential functions, or the nonlinear value of lost load), could involve more non-direct mission-related entities (such as childcare centers and base housing), and could include off-base communities that support mission-critical military personnel in line with the Office of the Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering energy resilience recommendations (DOD 2024). Additionally, power-hardware-in-the-loop testing and modeling systems allow for the physical replication of extreme grid disruptions such as power loss, frequency manipulation, and other anomalies that could arise from natural hazards or cyberattacks. These systems provide a realistic testing environment for simulating how advanced energy grids might behave under stress, allowing DOW to evaluate vulnerabilities that could impact military readiness. Moreover, simulations could model how outages affect military personnel, assets, and operations, as well as civilian infrastructure and stakeholders in theater. Simulations must consider traditional threats (such as adversary capabilities and logistical challenges) in concert with cyberattacks and factors such as DOW hardware capabilities, backup power sources, and the complex interdependencies among these components. Simulating the consequences of compounding natural hazards and cyberattacks could help DOW understand how grid failures could occur in tandem with other catastrophic events, potentially exacerbating their impacts. The resulting granular predictions could allow military planners to make informed energy resilience decisions. For example, a simulation might predict the number of military sorties impacted by power outages in a specific geographic region, thereby offering vital insights into operational impacts and the need for contingency plans. 6.6 Investments in Commercialized Technology Investments in existing advanced energy technologies could expand energy production, improve resilience, and reveal the best options for military applications. Expanded microgrid investments could enhance resilience and reduce dependence on external energy infrastructure, particularly in outage-prone or remote locations. To enable microgrid advantages, DOW could update its backup power requirements to specify the use of parallel-capable diesel generators (i.e., those equipped with controls and switchgear that enable integration and power sharing within microgrids). Any backup energy system that depends on fuel deliveries should also consider what constitutes an optimal level of on-site fuel storage, since emergency conditions may disrupt resupply. In contrast, energy sources such as geothermal, solar, wind, and advanced nuclear power could offer more resilient alternatives in contested or logistically constrained environments.
